bullets: A cactus stores water in a thick stem, a moth blends into bark, birds fly far for winter, and homes can be lost when people clear land
slides.heading: Adaptations: built to survive
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we meet adaptations - the special features that help living things survive - starting with a cactus in the dry desert, then a moth hiding on bark, birds flying far for winter, and finally what happens when people change animal homes.

bullets: Name the features that help a cactus survive in a hot, dry desert
Explain how camouflage keeps an animal safe and why birds migrate
Say why animal features are not chosen on purpose and what happens when people clear a forest
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to name a desert feature, explain camouflage and migration, and spot the mistake about animals choosing their features.

bullets: A pupil says a cactus grew its thorns because it wanted to keep animals away
Did the cactus really decide that, or did the feature develop another way?
slides.heading: Did the cactus choose its thorns?
slides.notes: Pose the claim from scene s1 without the verdict first: ask for a show of hands on whether a living thing can choose to grow a feature it needs, take two or three answers without judging them, and say scene s1 settles this exactly.

bullets: An adaptation is a special feature that helps a living thing survive in its home
Features such as thick stems, camouflage colours and long journeys all help survival
Features develop slowly over many generations - they are never grown on purpose
slides.heading: Features that help living things survive
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: an adaptation fits a living thing to its home so well that it can look chosen on purpose, but it developed over many, many generations, not by choice.

bullets: The cactus has a thick stem that stores water like a bottle for dry days
Its sharp thorns stop thirsty animals from biting it, and deep roots find water
slides.heading: Watch out: features are not grown by choice
slides.notes: Narrate the cactus as it appears in the animation: watch the thick stem fill with stored water, the thorns guarding it, and the deep roots reaching down - then hold up the warning that none of these features was grown by choice.

bullets: The moth's wings are the same colour as the tree bark it rests on
Hungry birds fly right past without seeing it, so blending in keeps it safe
slides.heading: Blending in keeps animals safe
slides.notes: Follow the moth on the bark: point to the matching wing colour, then watch the hungry bird fly past without spotting it - matching its home is called camouflage.

bullets: When winter comes, food becomes hard to find in the cold home
The birds fly thousands of kilometres to warmer places and return in spring
slides.heading: Birds travel far to survive
slides.notes: Trace the route arrow as the flock flies south: winter makes food scarce, so the birds travel far to survive, and they return when spring brings food back.

bullets: People sometimes clear forests to build farms and roads
When the trees go, the animals that lived there lose their food and shelter
slides.heading: People change animal homes
slides.notes: Watch the forest trees disappear one by one and the monkey move away: the animals did nothing wrong - their home was changed by people, so they lose food and shelter.

bullets: Start with the moth resting on the bark: its wings match the bark colour exactly
Because it blends in, the hungry bird cannot spot it, so camouflage keeps the moth safe
slides.heading: Worked example: why is the moth hard to spot?
slides.notes: Talk through scene s2 slowly and name each step: look at the wing colour first, compare it with the bark, then predict - the bird flies past because the moth blends in, and blending in is what keeps it safe.

bullets: Match each living thing to its survival feature: cactus, moth and migrating bird
Explain in one sentence why the cactus did not choose to grow its thorns
slides.heading: Your turn: match the features and explain the trap
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them to name the home each feature fits, and to explain that features develop over generations rather than by choice.

bullets: On your own: name one feature that helps the cactus survive in the desert
Say what camouflage is, and explain why an animal's feature is not grown by choice
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for a clear desert feature, a correct meaning of camouflage, and care with the trap - features developed over many generations, not by choice.
